utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Judge Nosworthy is unable to be with us for the remainder of this week for urgent personal reasons, but we have decided that it's in the interests of justice to continue in her absence, which we shall do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor Jokic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The examination by Mr. Zecevic will now continue. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, the question, yesterday, from His Honour Judge Chowhan, we heard the explanation, and that was the first time I myself heard it, that there is a difference between a mosque and a dzamija. During these proceedings so far, not a single witness used the term "moseja" in B/C/S, which is a mosque. Yesterday, when I looked at the list of registered immovable cultural property, and this list was drawn up between 1952 and 1994, until the 31st of December, 1994, I did not find a single building of Islamic provenance that is described as a moseja, or a mosque in English. Can you explain to me or do you have an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only explanation I have is the one I provided yesterday. I'm absolutely convinced that even the believers, religious believers from Kosovo and Metohija, do not know the difference between a dzamija and a mosque. Dzamija is the only term used by Albanians in Kosovo. I did hear of a term, moseja, but the dominant term used in daily communication is dzamija. I didn't find in the report of Mr. Herscher and Riedlmayer any mention of some moseja. This is why I did not pay attention to this difference in terminology.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now see P1773 on the left side of the screen and P2435 [as interpreted] on the right side, which is the mosque in Celine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's, I think, P2445, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I believe I said 2445. Maybe I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, this is the mosque in Celine, at least as shown by the experts of the OTP, Mr. Herscher and Riedlmayer. We spoke about that yesterday. In addition to these two photographs and the information provided here, the Prosecution provided also an excerpt from the land registry books from the cadastre concerning this particular building, and this is registered under number P2444.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's Exhibit P2444. Could we see that excerpt from the land registry books, P2444, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please comment this excerpt once it comes up on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could it be enlarged, please. Could it be enlarged just one more time, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you scroll up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. This is good enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Can you see this, Professor?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you comment on this possession list?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as far as I can see, this is an official possession list, and its main features are that it pertains to the Islamic community which is an owner of a certain plot of land located at the address Teha Selo Dzamija. Then, in the column culture name, it says "Shtepi". That means a house, a building.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, just a minute, please. This when it says culture name, it's the description of a type of dwelling built on that plot of land, and it says here a house, building?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely, that's how it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just slow down. It says here house, building; and then underneath it, it says a courtyard or a yard?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you saw other excerpts from the cadastre from the land registry books which pertain to religious buildings such as churches and mosques. In such excerpts from the cadastre from the possession list, in this column entitled culture name, does it normally say house, building, or something else?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on my experience and everything that I have done in terms of protecting cultural property, in all instances where a religious or a cultural property is involved, in this column it should say a monument or a religious building, not a house or a building because a house or a building is a broader term.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Does it say in certain excerpts a church, a mosque?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It certainly says a church or a mosque. For example, if you take the excerpt of the cadastre of the Bajrakli mosque in Pec, you will see that under the column culture name, it says a mosque; or in relation to some other sites, it will say a church. And in the documentation in these excerpts from the land registry books, you will definitely find such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: So if I understood you well, this possession list pertains to a house and a yard owned by the Islamic community in the Orahovac municipality, Celine village, located at the address Teha Selo Dzamija which is a house, a dwelling, and a yard, not a mosque?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, do you know how many entries in relation to Kosovo used the expression "mosque" in the register?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you've named one entry where the word or description "mosque" is used: The Bajrakli mosque in Pec. How many others are there recorded as mosques in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All mosques that were registered as cultural property, and they all have their possession list and I checked that. In the documentation, you will see that both those which are protected cultural property and those that are not will have that. There are 22 protected mosques, and I checked that, and all of them have their possession list, excerpts from the cadastre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And you say there are other entries in relation to mosques which are not protected mosques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is such an example. Messrs. Herscher and Riedlmayer included this mosque on their list, and we obtained a possession list and the possession list does not name it as such.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't think you understand my question. I want to know how many are registered as mosques. Is that only 22 or are there others which are described in the register properly as mosques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There certainly are. There are those which are not a cultural property. Only 22 mosques are a cultural property, but there are more as religious buildings. Among the 230 - there aren't 230; there are fewer of them - but among them, there are certainly mosques as religious buildings which have their own possession list, if the procedure was implemented, was completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you know how many there are?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I wouldn't be able to answer that question. This would be such a demanding task that a full team would need to work on it, to establish this fact, to visit all municipalities, to take out excerpts from all cadastre or land registry books, compare them, and then give you an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just gave you this as an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. There is one other matter. Of the 91 registered cultural properties of Islamic provenance, 22, you say, are mosques. What are the others in general terms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The other buildings are hammams, Kulas, Tekijas, and other buildings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry. Please continue, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One of the mosques -- or rather, one of the locations mentioned in our indictment is the town of Vucitrn. Messrs. Herscher and Riedlmayer, in their report, described the damage inflicted upon religious buildings in the town of Vucitrn. Since we looked at those mosques in Vucitrn and discussed them, could you give me your opinion, your view, on that part of the report by Herscher and Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When it comes to Vucitrn, it's a small town in the north of the province, 40 kilometres from Pristina towards Kosovska Mitrovica. In the report by Herscher and Riedlmayer, the report was done in such a way that the information on cultural property in Vucitrn was not systemitised. So there emerged a drastic example where existing cultural properties or cultural monuments were not included at all. This pertains to monuments both of Islamic and Christian provenance. We have an example that, in the report, they did not register the Nisan [phoen] of Mustafa Beg and the old hammam in Vucitrn. What is even more typical, the report does not include the oldest bridge, stone bridge, in the entire Serbia, and that is a monument of first category, of exceptional importance. And this monument dates from the 14th century, and it was built by the Vojnovic brothers who were nephews of Emperor Dusan. I'm sure that Riedlmayer and Herscher, if they visited Vucitrn at all, had to cross over that bridge because it is such a typical feature, such a unique feature, that anybody, especially anybody coming from elsewhere, has to notice it. There is also the Vojnovic Kula there, which is another protected monument.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Where is this in Professor's report, please, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't think, Your Honours, that the Professor included this in the report. We were just -- this is one of the examples which we were talking about. During the proofing sessions, we talked about the specific examples of Riedlmayer and Herscher report, where he should take the issue with, and it was Your Honours that insisted yesterday that we concentrate on the ones which are in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But he's not said a word about mosques in Vucitrn. We're talking about other things and we're talking about the inadequacies of their approach, but we've got loads of that criticism in here. If you are going to lead any more evidence from the witness, please try and help us with the specific instances we've heard about in the evidence, if you think he can assist us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I will, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have on our screens P1785. This is the mosque in Vlastica.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Professor, you will recall that we looked at this mosque in the village of Vlastica. Next to the photograph we have here, we will see the mosque as photographed by Mr. Sabri Bajgora. This photograph of the gutted interior, what does it tell you? Maybe you can comment on it.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult to give a comment on this photograph because you cannot identify a building if only part of the interior has been photographed. A photograph in itself is not a document in terms of protection. It has to be documented and accompanied by the relevant information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We've heard this repeatedly. We've got the point. We understand the point. Just assume for the moment that that's the mosque in Vucitrn -- sorry, in Vlastica, and tell us what you make of it. And if you can make nothing of it, say so and we'll move to something else.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot identify the building on the basis of this photograph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, let's move on then. If you're not going to comment on it, let's go to something you can comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have page 2 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just in case it's causing you anxiety, Professor, when it says: "Village atrocity caused by Serbs" on a photograph like that, we have no regard to that. We hear evidence about what may have happened. We don't accept what Riedlmayer says just because he's written on the document. There's no need for you to be so defensive about everything. Try to help us and we'll get to the truth, if we get the assistance of people. But we won't get to the truth if witnesses come here and tell us, Oh, well, the rules say such and such, therefore I can't tell you, I can't help you. You're an expert. You can tell us. It's obvious that's a mosque.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my only job and my greatest contribution would be if I were to convince you that complete confusion has been introduced by this lack of a methodological approach, and neither you nor I can enter into all the pores of this issue. It says, in the report, that there were ten buildings nobody visited, and yet they are included in the report, that only Mr. Bajgora visited a number of these, a hundred, in fact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Give us a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we do not want to hear any more evidence of a nature that is simply designed to criticise the methodology used by Riedlmayer and Herscher. We have a clear position of the witness on that, many examples. That subject's exhausted as far as we're concerned at this stage. If things arise in cross-examination, you can re-examine on them. If you have evidence to lead specifically related to the cases which are featured in the trial, please do so; otherwise, we will move to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't have, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. We'll move to cross-examination in that case, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there any Defence counsel wishes to question? No. So, you'll now be cross-examined by the Prosecutor, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Professor.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'd like to start some questions about your background and education that led up to your present status, and I'll start with your CV which is in your report at page 42 of the English. I think it's page 44 of the Serbian. And under university education, I see it says that you did basic studies in history in Pristina from 1968 to 1973, and you completed your basic studies in October 1973 and defended your diploma on relations of Serbia and Montenegro 1914 to 1918. I'm not the familiar with the education system in the former Yugoslavia. Can you tell me what degree that might be equivalent to in, for example, the United Kingdom or the United States? Is that equivalent to a master's degree, a bachelor's degree, a Ph.D.? Do you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The highest degree that you can get at university. I have a B.A. in history, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And you were a historian, plain and simple, right? You're not an art historian or an archaeologist or an anthropologist. You're a historian, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I am a historian; that's my educational background.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I see that your work experience then. Immediately after that, it appears that you worked as a professor of history and sociology at the Djordje Lopicic secondary school in Montenegro. What age are the students in the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's up to the age of 18; that's secondary education.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And then from 1979 to 1997, you were a professor of history at the TAM school centre in Slovenia. Can you tell me what kind of school that is? Is that a secondary school? Is that the same age group?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the same school, the same level, the same age group.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then in 1997 until 1998, you were a deputy general director of Panorama in Pristina. What was Panorama?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Panorama is a newspaper publishing company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of work did you do there?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a deputy to the general manager of Panorama, the director.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And as a historian, what kind of work were you doing as a deputy to the general manager?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did managerial work at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you had any prior experience or training as a manager?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You will allow me to say that I was able to do that because for 20 years I lived in an environment where the economy was paramount, and I gained experience there and went back to Panorama to help that company find a way out of the critical situation it was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand that. You, as I see, were a history professor at a secondary school for most of your work experience prior to that. In what way did you gain experience where the economy was paramount that led you to become a deputy manager?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you that that car factory was the largest car factory in the former Yugoslavia, and the school was part of that factory. It was part of the factory, and that kind of work required certain managerial knowledge because we, as a secondary school, also engaged in additional extracurricular activities, and there we gained experience and knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't see any reference here to a car factory here in your CV. It just listed you as a professor of history and sociology, that first year of 1973 to 1974, and then a professor of history and an educator from 1979 to 1997.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is the car factory in Slovenia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in Maribor. It was the largest car factory in the former Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- with 15.000 employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did you actually do any work or any managing in the car factory during 1979 to 1997?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a completely different method of managing.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Panorama was owned by who?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a state-owned company.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then from September 1998 until the present, you've been the director of the Pristina museum. How did you get that job in the first place?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I got that job in the regular way. After my predecessor left the post, there was a job vacancy, and I applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what prior experience did you have to be the director of a museum?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had sufficient experience certainly because history is a science that deals with economic history, culture, and so on, so that my knowledge of that field met all the criteria.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are you now or have you ever been a member of any political party?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never have I been a member of any political party.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One thing on your CV you list is that between 1974 and 1978 there was an interruption in your work because you were a political prisoner. For what had you been convicted that sent you to prison?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't only in 1974 to 1978, but also in 1971 to 1972, I was a political prisoner on two occasions, and I can list everything. I can tell you what this is about. In 1971, as a student, I was arrested and convicted. Today, we call this public speech, speaking in public. Today, it's difficult to comprehend, but in dictatorships that's what it's like. I was arrested for the same crime in 1974 and my indictment contained a single sentence, that I was the first accused at the trial of the students in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain, please. If I were now to give you for your inspection a book written by the chief of the counter-intelligence service of the State Security Service in Montenegro, who was the investigating judge who signed this document and who was in charge of the entire investigation, he sent me a copy of the book with a handwritten dedication, where he says that this is in memory of the time when one was not allowed to tell the truth. I received this book at the book fair in Podgorica when this man visited me, and his name is Vlado Kekovic. So everything I'm saying can be checked and verified.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, what was the nature of the anti-state activity or speech that you allegedly were engaged in? Isn't it because you were working against the majorization of the Albanian ethnic community in Kosovo? That's what it was about, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I was not working against out-voting or majorization. I was only asking for equal status in all the bodies and organs of the university for all ethnic groups studying at the university. It was not against something; it was for something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And it was because the Albanians were gaining a majority which made you, as a Serb, feel that you were being deprived of your rights; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have an impression; I knew the facts. You can find that in the documents of my trial, and you have all the statistics there. You had an organ at the university where there was 0 per cent or simply 2 or 3 per cent up to 10 per cent representative of all the groups at the university, and the Executive Board published this. The Executive Board of the province, the provincial government, published these statistics. So it's not something I produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, at that time, your views were seen as being contrary to the philosophy of the existing political powers about brotherhood and unity; correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you, and you have no reason to doubt what I'm going to say. I was fighting for equality which implies brotherhood and unity. It's not enough to use the slogan and say you're in favour of brotherhood and unity when matters stand completely differently. You will understand this because you come from a democracy and you live in a democratic society. So it's very hard for me to expect you to understand these problems which are very complex and very serious.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. On that same page in English, under your professional experience, you mention that you were coordinator of a travelling exhibition, jewellery and gold embroidery of Kosovo, between, here in the English translation, says 1993 to 1003 - I assume that means 2003 - which included, I guess, a show in Moscow. When was that travelling exhibition taken to Moscow?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't only in Moscow, it was in Finland. These were the two first international exhibitions in the history of the Pristina museum.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, but when was it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 2003 in Moscow, it was set up in the Konak of Countess Ljubica in Belgrade in 1998, and then it visited Moscow and Lahti.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On page 43 of the English, I suppose it's the next page of the B/C/S, under your bibliography, you list yourself as a professional collaborator, editor, and author of prefaces for publications. By my count, I see you down as a professional collaborator only one time, and that's in connection with something called the March Pogrom in Kosovo and Metohija 17 to 19 March 2004. That's the only time on this list that you worked as a professional collaborator, correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I signed the book, the March Pogrom. If I signed it, it means that I was the leader of the project, and publishers would know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, my question is: You are listed here as a professional collaborator and editor for that particular volume, but I see nowhere else -- I see nowhere else on this list where you're mentioned as a professional collaborator; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm the one who wrote all the introductory texts, who was in charge of the project. This may seem strange to you, but I coordinated and led all these activities, everything that's stated here.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For every single one of these items listed under 7.2, or are you only talking about the March Pogrom?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- no. I'm talking about all publishing projects and the projects we did on the protection of cultural heritage. Those were two types of projects: Projects in publishing, presenting and publishing; and also on the ground. It's a very complex job, including a large number of associates and assistants of various professional backgrounds, and there my managerial experience came in very useful because I was able to gather together all the different kinds of experts that were needed and compose a team.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you also say that you're the author of prefaces, in the plural, for publications. Under this list, I see the second one, Architectural Treasuries of Kosovo, and you are listed as the author of the preface. Were you the author of the preface for any of these other books, articles, et cetera, listed under the bibliography in 7.2, or is that the only one?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the only one. I also wrote a preface for the monography, Drenica: The Second Serbia Holy Mountain; then I wrote for a very important project monography Visoki Decani; and also many other of prefaces in a number of publications.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I know it may seem nitpicky, Professor, but you were rather nitpicky with the report of Messrs. Riedlmayer and Herscher, so I feel that I need to do it in their defence. You're not listed as the author of the preface for the article, Drenica: The Second Serbia --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll be very pleased to answer all of your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't have to ask these questions if you would put in your document which ones you were the author of the preface for. Let's go to 8.2, the bibliography in your report; page 46 in the English. By my count, there are some 57 different books, documents, articles listed there, and can you tell me are any of those by individuals who are not Serbs?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of the books listed here, there are no other authors apart from Serbian experts from Belgrade, but experts of other nationalities did cooperate with them: Hungarians, Roma, and others. But as we were dealing with the Serbian culture over the past ten years, quite naturally, the authors of these publications were Serbs. Unfortunately, that's how it was. I would have preferred to be able to establish cooperation with our Albanian colleagues with whom I had had excellent cooperation before, and we hope we will still have an opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: There was nothing to prevent you in preparing this report in having some cooperation with your former Albanian colleagues in Kosovo, was there? Could you not write them, e-mail them, telephone them?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I visited Pristina personally, Mr. Prosecutor, met with all my colleagues, visited the building I used to work in and my former office in Pristina. I visited them, I established contact with them. Of course, I was exported by Mr. Ral Bijali [phoen] of UNMIK, who was the chief of an UN UNMIK department, and I left them all my telephone number. Although my colleagues from the museum in Pristina do visit Belgrade on private business, they never do so on official business.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, have you ever testified before as an expert in any court before your testimony here this week?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is the first time I'm testifying in this form before a court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In preparing your report, what instructions did you receive about what you should write in your report?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In writing the report, in providing the evaluation, my main starting point were criteria and standards in the protection of cultural properties. I told you that my associates and I translated all of the documents from the Council of Europe concerning protection of cultural property. I also attended seminars where Messrs. Ball and Baccard gave lectures, and everything that concerns protection of cultural property, all the standards, all the professional experience applied in Europe, is something that I adopted from the beginning to the end in full. This is something that I'm well familiar with, and owing to that I was able to give appropriate guidance to our protection service. I hope that we will hold a seminar soon in Belgrade where our friends Ball and Baccard will come to teach because we established very good cooperation --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop. You're not answering my question any more. I understand why you would be considered an expert in identifying what the criteria and standards are for identifying cultural property and protective measures that might be needed, but is that what your instruction was about what you were supposed to write in your expert report for this trial?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The instruction was not along those lines. Nobody determined the methodology for me; I did it. I was to give evaluation, a professional evaluation, of the report by Herscher and Riedlmayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what materials did you review to prepare that report? I know you read their report or their survey. Did you look at the database that went along with that report, the IMG database?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used all available database, everything that was published in the last 50 years from the field of protection of cultural heritage. So I had a very detailed insight into the list of cultural properties in entire Serbia, including Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But my specific question was: Did you look at the IMG database that Herscher and Riedlmayer used or incorporated, included, with their report?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was guided, first and foremost, by the database accepted by UNESCO and everything used by UNESCO in their reports, in their research in Kosovo and Metohija --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, no. Please, stop. Can you answer my question: Did you look at the IMG database referred to by Riedlmayer and Herscher in connection with their report? Do you know if you looked at that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not look into that database. I looked into the content of the report. That's what I evaluated.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you not think it might be helpful in evaluating their report if you looked at the database that they referred to and used in connection with their report?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably would have been good had it been available to me; it wasn't available to me. All other reports were available to me, and I used about seven of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Why wasn't it available to you? Did you ask for it from the lawyer over there?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had available to me what was presented to me as the subject of the report by Riedlmayer and Herscher.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, in reading Riedlmayer's report, did you not see a reference to that database? Let me withdraw that and ask you the question this way. In page 18 of the English of Riedlmayer and Herscher's report, paragraph A2.2, he makes reference to the EU IMG database and explains it. So, if you read his report, you must have seen that, but you didn't ask your lawyer if you could get a copy of it, a copy of the CD?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, at first, I read the report by Riedlmayer and Herscher. Given the nature of their report, given that they were not an official team or not officially included in the work by Riedlmayer and Herscher, I did not use that report. I had available to me the book by Bajgora, and I can't comment on it professionally because it's not suitable.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, that strikes me as strange if your task was to do a review or an evaluation of Herscher and Riedlmayer's report. They make specific reference to this EU IMG database and they say it's attached to the report and a copy of the database is available on a CD. You didn't think it was necessary or helpful or important to you in making an evaluation of their report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I evaluated the methodology used by Riedlmayer and Herscher as stated by them in the very beginning of their report, and that was the guiding principle in my work. Mr. Riedlmayer and Herscher did not state in their document that this organization or this expert team was part of their team, so that information was relevant to me. They were included only subsequently into the project by Herscher and Riedlmayer; that wasn't the starting point.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What languages to you speak, read, and understand? I know Serbian. Albanian?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I used to speak Albanian quite well. But given that I left the area quite early and then spent many years in Slovenia, I forgot some of it and there were also some changes in the official language. I understand it well. I speak Slovenian. I used to speak good German. Before, I spoke a bit of a lot of languages, but nothing quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you, in preparing your report, have the opportunity to review the trial testimony of Mr. Riedlmayer in the Slobodan Milosevic case?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not have occasion to study it in detail, just excerpts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how about his testimony in this case against Mr. Milutinovic and the others?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I apologise. I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How about Mr. Riedlmayer's testimony in this case against Mr. Milutinovic and the others, did you have a chance to review that testimony?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Not at all?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If I can Your Honours' indulgence for a moment, that raises something I need to check for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Isn't there a paragraph in your report where you have a cite to a part of Mr. Riedlmayer's testimony in this case? I would refer you to it looks like page 17 of your report in the B/C/S. It's section 5.4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, in the English, this is at page 16.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you find that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. Will you assist me again, please, and tell me which page it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I believe there was a paragraph number, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's paragraph number 5.4 immediately below your table 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On my copy here, the page number is listed as 5.4-17; and in e-court, I think it's page 17 of the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean, "The critical approach in selecting sources ..." Yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. You see the second paragraph there. My English translation says: "On 30 October 2006, during testimony in this case, IT-05-87-T, Mr. Riedlmayer said he had wanted to establish contact with UNESCO experts," and then there's a quotation in English apparently from his testimony on that day, right? Is that what it says in your copy?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, if that's not what it says in your copy, then I'm curious to see what you're looking at that's different from what's filed in e-court. Could you have a look at the screen in front of you. On the left is the page that I'm looking at, and that second paragraph reads -- it has an English quotation in it. You see that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So if what you just told us, that you never read or saw or heard Mr. Riedlmayer's testimony in this case, how did you get this quotation and this remark referring to his testimony on 30 October 2006 in your report?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't follow the entire testimony. We studied certain statements, but I didn't have the entire document before me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you read and understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "On 30th of October, 2006, during testimony in this case, Mr. Riedlmayer said that he wanted to English contact with UNESCO experts." I don't understand this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on. Could you answer my question: Do you understand English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When you read excerpts from the trial of Milosevic, in what language were you reading these excerpts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have my associates, my aides, who translate texts in English for me, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis, we don't have the explanation yet for this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's outstanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I need to follow-up on a couple things of what Judge Bonomy asked you. Your associates who translated for you regarding the Milosevic --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: By your leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This particular instance, we took it as something quite telling because we established contact with Mr. Ros Borath, who was in Pristina at the time when Riedlmayer and Herscher were there, and we personally saw him when we were in Pristina, and I --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. That's not answering my question. Let me go back. First of all, let me follow-up on what Judge Bonomy asked you. You just said that regarding the excerpts from Milosevic, some of your associates helped translate for you. What document were they reading from? It was my understanding that the Milosevic transcripts were only in English; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the legal service provided that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what language was the transcript from the Milosevic trial from which you reviewed excerpts with the help of your assistants?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it was in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, the next thing I want to clear up with you. I asked you earlier, I said: How about Mr. Riedlmayer's testimony in this case against Mr. Milutinovic and the others, did you have a chance to review that testimony?" Your answer: "I didn't." I said: "Not at all?" And you said: "I didn't." And now you just said, well, you looked at some excerpts like this one that's in here. Which is it? Did you review it not at all or did you look at some excerpts?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I understood you to mean whether I followed in the entirety the testimony, and my answer to that was no. We did not understand each other. I only looked at what I was interested in concerning the problem of the presence of UNESCO representative in Pristina. I believe that to be important.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, please, you didn't understand me when I said: "Not at all"? You didn't understand what that term meant?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is clear that we didn't understand each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think something's clear, but I think you understood me. Then when I showed you this article in this portion in your statement, where it's obvious that you must have seen some of the transcript, you had to change your answer. That's what happened, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please allow me to explain. I had occasion to familiarize myself with this because this is the centre for -- or rather, the centre for preserving Kosovo and Metohija established contact with Ros Borath, and that's what I had in mind. I touched upon the Riedlmayer and Herscher report only in relation to that particular segment; nothing more than that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Could I please see the copy, the hard copy of the report, that you're reading from, Professor. Professor, would you please give to the usher --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- your copy. The hard copy, would you hand it to him, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Usher, could you return that, please, to the witness. Thank you. If you look at your hard copy and look at what's on the screen, you will see that they are different in the format and that at least part of the first paragraph in your copy does not appear in the copy on the screen. Now, you've obviously got a copy that's been at a different stage of preparation from the one that is officially in use in the trial. Can you tell us whether the one you have in your hand is a later version or an earlier version?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can't say with certainty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, we've been very trusting throughout this trial, unlike I'm sure other Trial Chambers on occasions, and have just accepted that the binders being handed to the witnesses matched the material before the Court on e-court. There may be little in this for all I know because certainly the bit that Mr. Hannis is concentrating on does appear in both, but it's not satisfactory if they are not identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, let me, first of all, we didn't provide any binders because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So where did this copy come from?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe the witness brought it with him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- which is why I really cannot help at this point, I cannot be of any help to the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, do you have anything to say on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour. When we started yesterday, I provided him a copy of the B/C/S version I have, which matches what's in e-court, and he started out with that. Then we had a break and the Defence asked if one could be substituted. I guess that's the one he had with him, but I don't know why that occurred and I don't know what the differences are. Maybe it's minimal, maybe it's nothing, but not knowing is troubling.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, my understanding is that it is the exact, exact copy, only all in Serbian, because in the document which is before us in the e-court, we have some parts which are original from the Herscher/Riedlmayer report. That was for the benefit of the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the one that the witness has is a track-change version, which therefore includes bits which have been deleted before, obviously, a final version was compiled, but it still has material in that first paragraph not apparently deleted which doesn't appear in the one on the screen. The usher will show it to you so that you can see what I'm referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. If you put it on the ELMO, that might be the best way and then everyone can see it. Now, if you look at the last sentence of the first paragraph, that's before the part that's set in, am I right - I may be wrong, so we need to clarify this first of all - am I right in thinking that that last sentence --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Is not in the definite report, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And only part of it's been deleted?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I believe the whole sentence after table 4 has been deleted; two sentences, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But they have, in fact, from the one on the screen, but they're still there in this one; and, in fact, the last two lines of that paragraph are not underlined as if they had been deleted at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I really cannot help you, Your Honours, with that because, I mean, if I would -- if I would have the opportunity to look at the document, I can probably provide you with some explanation. I don't really, at this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we're going to do is let Mr. Hannis look at the copy that the witness has had in his hand during the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, meanwhile, we'll remove it, the usher will give it to Mr. Hannis, and we will use only the screen for any references. So we will confine our attention to what's in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is it the whole report you intended me to have, Your Honour, or only a page?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I think Mr. Hannis should have the whole of that copy, so that he can see what differences there may have been referred to. This arises only because it's been used in the course of the evidence; otherwise, it could remain confidential. But because it's become an issue in the presentation of the evidence, then it's necessary for the Prosecutor to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Professor, for a little bit we'll have to continue then with what's on the screen, and my question -- my next question for you is then: Is it your testimony that you only looked at a few excerpts from the testimony of Professor Riedlmayer in this case and not his entire testimony?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reviewed the entire Riedlmayer/Herscher report; but as for the testimony, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But how did you find this particular excerpt in order to put it in your report? Did somebody else do that for you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this excerpt was very interesting to me, and that's why I used it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that, but how did you find it? You told us you don't read English that well, and you told us you didn't review the whole thing. So how did you find these three little sentences out of Mr. Riedlmayer's testimony, which went over two days or two and a half days? How did you find this little gem?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My translator. While I was working on the report, I received this from my translator.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how did your translator know to pick out this one?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My translator worked on this project together with me. I had to consult my translator concerning all the terminology in the report and in all the searches.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what's the name of your translator? We can go into private session if you want.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mrs. Milica Sefkusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And did she read the entire testimony of Professor Riedlmayer from his testimony in this trial?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, was she reading the English transcript?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She recommended this part to me as very characteristic, and I accepted it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's not my question. That's not my question. My question is: Was she reading an English transcript of the testimony in this case?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's my understanding the only other version we have is a French version. Does she speak and read French?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She does, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know if she was reading the French version of the transcript?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know which --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know because, well, English was the primary language used in the whole procedure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know whether she's better in English or in French?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: She's better in English.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The reason I ask is this a quotation which purports to be from Professor Riedlmayer on the 30th of October, 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would direct you to the transcript at page 5414 from the 30th of October, 2006, beginning at line 14. And I will avow to the Court, and I'm sure my colleagues on the otherwise can call me to task if I'm wrong, but my review of the transcript on that day, there are only three references to UNESCO. All three of them are in this paragraph between lines 14 and 21. You will see that, while generally it's talking about the same thing, there are several differences between what's in the transcript and what's quoted in English in the Professor's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Who put this English in your report? Is that what your translator provided to you? Did she type that in?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall precisely because the material was voluminous. I was interested in the crux of the matter. That's what I concentrated on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, yes, but you take Mr. Riedlmayer and Mr. Herscher to task over all kinds of things in their report, and you as an expert are presenting this report with inaccurate information. You're quoting Mr. Riedlmayer, purportedly, and this is not what he said. That's not very professional of you, is it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I didn't comb through this. I simply put forward the most elementary information. Had I gone into meticulous detail, I would have had to list facts for a month. I just focused on the most important matters. I didn't split hairs because I know that in every job there can be omissions, there can be errors, and anyone can make a mistake including me. But it's true that the representative of UNESCO was in Pristina, it's true that we communicated with him --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop. That's not an answer to the question. Are there any other portions of the report that you personally did not write, or is all the rest of it your own work?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's all my work, but you'll agree that no one could work on a report by himself. A person needs a translator and a typist to work on the computer. This is an enormous job. I accept everything in here as mine. I'm just explaining to you --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But what you can't --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I'm not denying that this is my report. This is certainly my report. If there's a technical error, it doesn't impinge on the crux of the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, sir, if there are enough technical errors would you agree with me it raises concerns about the overall report?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, absolutely. I allow that the entire report must be evaluated, but I'm deeply convinced that I did everything here with the best of intentions and attempting to avoid any possible mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If there are errors, I accept that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's time for the break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, we have to have a break at this stage, that will be for 20 minutes. While we have the break, could you please leave the courtroom with the usher, and we will resume at ten minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, before the witness comes in, in all fairness to the witness, we have identified the part which is in the transcript. It is not the 30th but the 31st, and it's 5586, line 3 to 7. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic brought that to my attention, Your Honour, and I apologise. I had no intent to mislead anybody.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I resume?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, before we started, I just want to tell you that I may have been too hard on it because it's been brought to my attention during the break that that English quotation, indeed, is in Mr. Riedlmayer's testimony, but on the 31st of October rather than the 30th. So the error in your report is the date rather than the content. I want to ask you about some additional items in your report, however. On page 10 of the English, and I'm not sure what page it is in the B/C/S. It's item number 4 regarding approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And while we're waiting for that, Your Honour, I would indicate that we have had a chance now to do a quick check of the hard copy that the Professor was using. We note some minor differences in phraseology in a number of places. They don't seem to change the overall content of what's there, but there are some parts marked with track changes and other parts as well. During the break, we weren't able to do much more. But, you know, based on previous dealings with counsel on the other side, I don't have a serious concern about that, other than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. So this can now be returned to Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And if the witness is to use a hard copy, he should use the one that Mr. Hannis gave him at the outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: By all means, Your Honour. The relevant copy is in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's the one which we relied on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But it expedites the proceedings when a witness has a hard copy. We appreciate counsel have noted of that and made use of them when appropriate, so we will try to restore the situation we had at the beginning of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Does the witness, in fact, still have that copy or was it returned?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have the hard copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, let's give it back to the witness in case it should help him to find the appropriate parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, it's page number 10 in English, and I'm not sure which page it is in your hard copy. It's fairly close --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's the same page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And my question has to do with the last paragraph, where you say: "Because the report that is the subject of our evaluation was prepared with the instructions of representatives of international institutions of justice ..." My question is: What do you base that on, that Riedlmayer and Herscher's report was prepared with instructions of international -- representatives of international institutions of justice?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This statement is based on what is stated in Mr. Riedlmayer and Herscher's report. They say that themselves at the beginning of their report; and, of course, it's quite natural. They were given a certain task, but probably they were limited in their work by the nature of the task they were given.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, can you indicate to me precisely what instructions you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, precisely the instructions they themselves report in their report. That's the only information I was able to use concerning this. We did not go outside the context of what they themselves said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, can you point me to a page or paragraph in the report. Maybe it's there. I'm just not finding it. There is a paragraph in page 3 of the English version of the report. It says: "Following a briefing by the staff of the OTP, they proceeded to Kosovo and carried out field investigations." But I don't read that as saying they had instructions. Is that what you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And since you didn't read the testimony of Mr. Riedlmayer in this trial, you don't know what he had to say about that at pages 5420 through 5421 in this case, do you? You can just answer yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll save that one for later. You talk about their sources, and I'm looking at page 19 of the English now. I'm not sure what page it is for you. The left-hand column has a reference to A2.14, media accounts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's page 20 of the Serbian.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you indicate that the media are unreliable sources. I agree with you that often that's true. Do you find no media sources to be reliable?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that not a single media report is reliable. But from experience, especially when there's a war on, you yourself know that, in wartime situations, newspaper reports are often incorrect, and that's maybe natural in view of the circumstances the journalists have to work in. I only felt that newspaper articles cannot be considered relevant if such an important assessment has to be made. One then has to have reliable sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Right above that, in my English version, you're talking about documentation by photographs. You say: "Photography cannot be an independent means of verification because a photograph itself is not a document without interpretation." In English, we have a saying that a picture is worth a thousand words. Isn't it true that oftentimes a photograph speaks volumes?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A photograph can certainly say a lot; but if it is not accompanied by the proper description, it can often be seriously misleading. If a photograph contains certain interpretations, certain markers in it, then it can, indeed, be relevant information.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Immediately above that, there is a reference to the Serbian Orthodox Eparchy of Raska-Prizren, and your evaluation says: "Avoiding confident informants from the Serbian side ..." What proof do you have to support that claim that Herscher and Riedlmayer were avoiding competent informants from the Serbian side?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, this example illustrates our objectivity. We did not accept information coming from the Serbian Orthodox church as relevant because we don't consider them to be -- well, we don't consider a monk to be an expert source who knows about the protection of the cultural heritage. So Mr. Riedlmayer and Herscher could have established contact. We met Mr. Herscher in Decani monastery and offered him our cooperation, and I wish we had worked on this together.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When was it you met Mr. Herscher at Decani?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When in 2000?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know whether it was autumn or early spring of 2001, but it was around that time because we visited Decani more than once.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And who spoke with him and offered their assistance? Was that you personally?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally was there with Mrs. Menkovic, who is the president of the centre for the preservation of the heritage of Kosovo and Metohija. We were in charge of the project of urgent protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The only documented indication I've seen in your report and the attached annexes about efforts on your side to contact Herscher or Riedlmayer is one -- a photocopy of what appears to be an e-mail exchange with Mr. Herscher in, I think, the end of October 2001. I would suggest to you that by then Herscher and Riedlmayer had already finished writing their report. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Communication by e-mail came about later, but before that we had met in the field. Communication followed when there appeared to be no prospects of cooperation, so e-mails were sent by both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You never had any contact with Mr. Riedlmayer, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with Mr. Riedlmayer because we didn't have an opportunity, and we met Mr. Herscher by accident. We ran into him by accident because we didn't know where they were going.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could go to the next page or the next entry after the media accounts that we started with, it's A3.2.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And now we're on page 20 of the English, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Reports by Kosovar refugees, eye-witness accounts were used, and you say this is unreliable and incompetent sources. Under your argumentation, you say: "One cannot expect a refugee to be an objective witness ..." Is that your position, sir, that no refugee can be an objective witness?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't say that there are no such persons. Certainly, there are objective persons among them, but allow me to say that they're in a special situation where it's natural that emotions are present. And if there are emotions, you can imagine what kind of statements can be made because such sources in the nature of things are unable to control themselves and be objective. That's quite natural, it's normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you're saying over half a million, hundreds of thousands of refugees from Kosovo cannot be objective witnesses about cultural damage, about destruction of mosques in their own villages? Is that your position?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You misunderstand me. I'm sorry. I didn't -- I wasn't referring to that number, but to the number surveyed while the work on the report was going on. That's what I was referring to. To make that kind of analysis is something that a sociologist should do. This is a problem of sociology which I didn't go into. I only made an assessment based on the report because if you read the comments that the person surveyed said, you'll see the statements are incomplete. They are ad hoc, they have no grounds, they don't identify the building, the time. Not a single person who answered the survey provided complete and full information, at least as Mr. Herscher and Riedlmayer's -- as far as that report is concerned, because it deviates from their goal?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you know what their goal was? What do you believe their goal was?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Their goal was to establish the actual situation when it comes to the destruction of the cultural heritage and religious buildings; although, the definition of the religious heritage is incomplete, in my opinion, here because we could discuss that. What the religious -- what the cultural heritage encompasses, this is only part of it, the part covered by the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: As I understand it of what you said yesterday, you said you don't dispute that destruction occurred, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not dispute that at all. I just want it to be specific, and I want it to be documented as to the numbers, destruction, and so on. We need to establish the truth, and the truth can only be established if we use the accepted standards. We should not skip over accepted procedures that have been used in profession for dozens of years and that have provided good results.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And in preparing your report and your evaluation of Herscher and Riedlmayer's work, you didn't read the transcripts of the testimony in this case from eye-witnesses to damage to mosques in their villages, did you? You didn't read the testimony of Sabri Popaj or Agim Jemeni about the mosque in Celine, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, you have. Well, wait a second. How much testimony in this case have you read? I thought you told us only excerpts and only what your translator brought to you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read statements of a couple of witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which ones?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- based on which, well, what was available to me. I can't remember the exact names, but I remember that there was a very characteristic testimony about a building in Smolnica.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I know you have not testified as an expert in trial before, but I would suggest to you, sir, that it's a common practice with many experts in preparing expert reports to list in their own report all the materials that they've read and relied on in preparing their report. There's nothing in your report about reading testimonies or statements of witnesses who claim to have eye-witness information about cultural damage. Can you tell me now how many such statements you read and the names of the persons whose statements you read?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My primary goal or my primary preoccupation was to establish the list of cultural properties, to identify cultural properties, and to make a conclusion based on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, sir, stop.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't go into --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're not answering my question. Did you not understand it? Do I need to ask it again?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what else to tell you. I really wasn't focused on that, what you're saying. My attention wasn't focused on the legal aspect of the report, but on something that concerns the --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. My question is: Can you tell me how many such statements you read and the names of the persons whose statements you read? Can you tell me that, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't remember the names. It's hard for me to remember the names, especially since --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you write that down somewhere?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly did in the material that I used as a basis for writing my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You don't have a copy of that with you, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's work material.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any other kind of work material that you read and relied on in making this report that is not referred to in your report?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that I've mentioned almost all kinds of material in my report. Perhaps I omitted some minor ones, but the essence is in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whatever I considered relevant I listed in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you considered the statements of eye-witnesses to cultural damage something minor that didn't need to be listed in your report?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I meant, Mr. Prosecutor. I believed that I shouldn't be assessing witness evidence. It is not up to me to do that. It is up to me to deal with the strictly professional issues. I didn't focus on legal side of it, and I think it's understandable. I didn't want to go into that because that's slippery ground for me, and I would never allow myself to evaluate something that goes beyond my professional expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The next entry below that - actually, two below that - number 5, witness interviews, your evaluation is: "Witness interviews were taken without attempting even to satisfy ethnic balance ..." Is there some protocol that requires interviews to be taken from an equal number of people from all ethnicities? What's your reason for this criticism?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not what I meant. I didn't mean that the number of surveyed witnesses needed to be equal. I think that's not possible either. But one can always look for a ratio that would be acceptable in order to confirm this. In order for the report to be more relevant, it would need to use a greater number of sources when it comes to witnesses because everybody saw it from their own angle. Everybody saw it with their own eyes, and there were a lot of such examples.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. On page 21 of the English, this is under item 5.5, general accomplishment of assigned goals, you're talking about: "This was too short a time for such a serious task." This is where you talk about how many structures Riedlmayer and Herscher gathered data on, with your breakdown of how many they would have had to see in the days they were present in the territory. At the bottom of your argumentation about that, you say: "In a large number of cases, the structures in the field were visited by two individuals; an individual and an institution or two institutions in various time-periods, A. Herscher and A. Riedlmayer, never visited any single site together ..." You're wrong about that, sir. What was your basis for writing that in your report?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The basis was precisely the report by Riedlmayer and Herscher because after touring each building, they would write down who toured it and who produced the photographs. And based on that, I drew my conclusions because on each site, you can see who the author of the photograph was and who visited the site. And in relation to ten sites or 11 sites, I didn't find any information indicating of who toured it. That means that they weren't toured, at least that's what the documentation says. That doesn't necessarily need to be accurate. You will find that data towards the end of the report where there are several buildings on the same location that had not been toured. I'm just saying this so you can find it easier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.
