But if you had read the testimony of Mr. Riedlmayer in this case, you would know that he testified under oath on the 31st of October, at page 5541, lines 17 through 20: "At the time that we received the information, Mr. Herscher and I visited every site together, and we could usually have a division of labour: One of us would handle the camera, the other one would be recording information ..." He also said the same thing basically, at page 5450, lines 11 through 17. But because you didn't read the testimony of Mr. Riedlmayer, you got that wrong in your report, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't write it erroneously. I simply evaluated what they put in their report. In the report itself, you can see for yourself that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yeah, but you're wrong. They both visited every site, and you say they didn't visit a single site together. How more wrong can you be?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I now can go over the table with 230 buildings that they offered in their report. I can do it now, and I had no reason to think that they would make such a mistake in their report. I simply took this report as a product of their work. I had no reason to suspect that they put it down erroneously. A mistake or two, that's possible. They were put in -- they came as a result of a chance, and they're quite evident in the report. Let me just give you an example.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no. Stop. Don't give me an example because I didn't ask you that question. The lawyer over there might ask you about it when it's his turn again. Might point is, sir, you've written a report purporting to be an expert and your report is criticising the report of Riedlmayer and Herscher. The point I'm trying to make is you knew that Riedlmayer came here to testify about his report. You were aware of that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you think it would be helpful to you in preparing an evaluation of his report to hear what he had to say under oath when he testified here? You didn't think you needed to see that? You didn't think that might enlighten you about some ambiguities that you saw in the report?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I primarily did not consider Mr. Riedlmayer's testimony as something that should be my focus because that was in another case, if you had in mind the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no. I'm talking about his testimony in this very same case. You didn't think it would be helpful to see what he had to say about his report, not just in Milosevic but in this case as well?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can just repeat that I believed that I shouldn't deal with those kinds of issues. My main guiding point was their report. I based my work on their report. I didn't think that I needed to evaluate issues that are dealt with by the Court. I think that it is up to the Court to deal with it, not up to me. That was my position.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One of the issues being dealt with by the Court concerning Mr. Riedlmayer was his report. Let me give you one concrete example, and I'll stop on this. Would you agree with me, at least, it would have been helpful to you to have read Mr. Riedlmayer's testimony in this case because then you would not have made the mistake that you did make putting in your report that Riedlmayer and Herscher never visited a single site together? If you had read the testimony, you wouldn't have written that in your report, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it comes to evaluating a report, then I can't agree with you; otherwise, I would. But my task was to evaluate their report, so I cannot take it upon my shoulders to be responsible for the form in which the report was provided. The report was the basic document that I was to evaluate, in my mind. Let me just say. Take Landovica as an example. Mr. Riedlmayer was in Landovica --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. You've answered my question. Your lawyer can ask you something further if he wants. Were you paid by the hour or were you paid a flat fee for your work?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a flat fee.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So by not taking the time to read two and a half days of transcript, you made more money per hour that way, right?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I would need to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: On what basis?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, my learned friend knows -- just a second. My learned friend knows the way how OLAD is paying for all experts and there is really nothing that we can do because that's a policy of this Tribunal, and it assumes what it assumes as obligation of any expert and everybody is paid the same fee and same amount.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On page 29 of the English, sir, and I'm not sure what page that is for you, it has to do with an evaluation about the 49 Islamic monuments in Pec and Peja.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if my learned friends can help me with the B/C/S page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's page 30.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you find that, Professor?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Riedlmayer and Herscher say that every one of the district's 49 Islamic monuments was attacked, and they go on a bit. In your evaluation, you say: "All," all, "such data are totally unprofessional, unverifiable, and unreliable. Nowhere else is there information that there were 18 mosques from the 15th, 18th centuries in Pec. The hammam is certainly not from the 15th century because there exists documentation about it as a cultural property." I'm not sure what that means. You said: "The hammam is not from the 15th century because there exists documentation about it as a cultural property." Does that documentation say it's from a later date, or is it because it's designated cultural property that means it's newer? What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It means that "in the existing documentation" there is a list of monuments, the one that you used yesterday. In there, you will find that hammam is registered as a cultural property, and that it is from the 17th century. I took that as an example of the erroneous approach and arbitrary attitude in giving assessments. This was an example because you may say two centuries doesn't mean much when it comes to historical heritage, but this is just an example based on which you can come to doubt other data for which there is no documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is why --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your disagreement, then, is with their dating of some of the buildings that they describe, but you don't dispute that those buildings were damaged or destroyed, as described in the report, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Based on the entire report, you can see that due to inconsistencies confusion is created, and then nobody is sure, nobody is certain, of the data offered. I would truly like to find an expert who could, based on the documentation offered when it comes to these 40-some buildings in Pec, an expert who could come up with a relevant figure when it comes to cultural and religious property.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you personally don't have any information to dispute or refute what Riedlmayer and Herscher have to say about that number of monuments, mosques, et cetera, being damaged or destroyed?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I consulted all existing documentation, everything that exists, and I did not come to that conclusion. You may believe me or you may decide not to believe me. I was born in Pec, I know every street and every alley, and I'm familiar with all of these locations. These figures are not conducive to finding a stability in the future because every manipulation will produce a counter manipulation, and that won't do us any good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what is your position? Are there or are there not 36 mosques?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, there aren't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How many are there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only offer you information connected to the sources in the documentation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Well, how many are there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About ten, a dozen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And your entire basis for saying that is that that's the total number that are registered in documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not in a position now, you'll allow me to say, that I'm not in a position to protect my profession. I feel very uncomfortable if I have to say something off the top of my head. If there was documentation to be consulted, all the information would have to be correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can you answer my question. The entire basis for your conclusion about the number of mosques in Pec is the number actually registered in documents, or am I misunderstanding you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the only relevant information for cultural goods is what is registered as a cultural property. Religious properties also have to be registered with the Islamic community.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you prepared to answer my question or not? Please don't try to defend what you've done. Just answer the question. I'm not accusing you of doing anything wrong. I only want to know whether the entire basis for saying that there are ten or a dozen mosques is that that's the total number that are registered in documents in Pec. And if I'm wrong that that's the basis you're using, please tell me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely. The information offered is incorrect. I don't have any information to confirm anything like this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand why you can't just answer my question and why you have to go racing off onto something else. Let's move on. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour, please may I add something.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm reminded that that's the basis on which you make this conclusion in spite of the fact that you know every street and every alley and you're familiar with all the locations and you were born there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. That's my free assessment, that there aren't that number of mosques. But I ask you very kindly if I may just say one thing. I feel very uncomfortable when something that is the result of professional work over 40 or 50 years is brought into question. If one day the Serbian Orthodox church asks a similar question and says there was so much of all that, we know it was there, but they don't offer any documentation, then we have two opposing sides and we will never be able to overcome this. There will never be any degree of understanding or reconciliation. Things should not be made up or confused, and that's my main goal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Sorry, Professor. I wish to intervene and inform you that when you are here to depose, you have to talk of the ground realities and merely not anchor all your information coming from a particular official source, because you've taken the oath of telling us everything that is correct. You know that place very well, you have lived there. That is the why you have to tell us the realities. That's where there's testimony; otherwise, we could get the record and read it. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think two more things from your report, Professor, and then I'll move on to a different topic. I'm now back at page 18 of your report. This is under table 4. I think it's the third entry under table 4. That's probably page 18 or 19 for you. You're talking about, with regard to documentation on mosque, you found that some facts directly refute these biassed conclusions, and they're just that photo documentation that the authors are constantly citing. In your argumentation, you point to a specific example concerning the burning of the office and archive of the Islamic community in Pristina on 13 June. You say that NATO forces had entered Kosovo and Metohija on the 12th of June, 1999; and before then, all police forces had to leave Pokrajina. Serbian police would have had to set the fire in the presence of a large number of people and of NATO forces. You say all police forces had to leave. Let me ask you this: When did you personally leave Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't leave, I just withdrew temporarily, and this was in mid-August or towards the end of August 1999 municipal.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So were you in Pristina town on the 13th of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, I was. I'm aware of that incident because it was near my institution, and one could see everything from the window of my office.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you saw it burning on the 13th of June, 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did. I saw people gathering. I saw there was a crowd, people were passing by the building, they were curious, but I didn't leave my office. I just looked out of my office window.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you were aware that police were still in Pristina town on the 13th of June, 1999, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Anyone who was on the spot can confirm there was no chance that on the 13th of June the police could have been in Pristina. It was technically impossible because KFOR had taken all the -- had taken up all the buildings on the first day.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You say anyone on the spot would have known? That's what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I'm saying that if anyone who was there at that point in time, anyone who was there could tell you that there was no possibility of the police moving around the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You weren't aware of a Reuters news report from the 13th of June about the British paratroopers shooting a man who had first approached them and fired shots at them; and they, those British troops, consulted with MUP police about that event on the 13th of June? You didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't know about that, but believe me --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop, stop, stop. I just asked you if you knew. If you don't know, that's fine. I'll move on to something else. You didn't know about a Cox news service report from the 13th of June, 1999, from Marsha Kunstel, about the Russians who were at the Pristina airport? Did you know about that, some 300 Russian troops dug-in at the airport, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of that, yes. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware that Serbian police prevented reporters from approaching General Michael Jackson while he tried to give a conference at the airport? You didn't know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You weren't aware of Washington Post report about Yugoslav soldiers and Serbian police still in evidence in many areas in the capital, Pristina, on the 13th of June?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can tell you that if we were to use media sources, they were contradictory. Media sources from all sides were contradictory.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please just answer the question. Don't you understand the concept of answering the questions you're asked?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So I take it you don't know about that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, specifically --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, hold on, Mr. Hannis. Mr. Zecevic is concerned about something.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours. I was just wondering what is the basis of all these questions about, and I assume that's media reports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: He's asking on that basis to show he's got a foundation for asking the question. He knows very well that that doesn't make it evidence, but he's doing it so that you won't get up and say what's his basis for asking that question. It's been done many times so far in the trial. Can anyone help with the answer to the question at line 23, and the reference to Serb police preventing reporters from approaching General Jackson at the airport? Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, lastly, specifically relating to the Islamic community's archives, were you aware of a report by Janine Di Giovanni for the Times of London on the 14th of June, indicating that: On the 13th, under the nose of recently arrived NATO, the two-storey hall of records which houses all the documents from the grand mosque was torched and burned to the ground. Eye-witnesses too frightened to give their names said they saw two civilian cars with around 15 policemen run into the house; and when they came out, the house burst into flames." You never heard about that one?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, your --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes or no, did you? Did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's technically impossible to do that, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's technically impossible to say whether you heard about it or not? I'm just asking you yes or no.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't hear about it because it's not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no, no. I didn't ask you that. I asked you yes or no. Please just answer yes or no. Don't add your editorial comment.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. You'll be happy to hear the last thing I want to ask you about in your report is on page 34 of the English, and that may be page 35 for you. It concerns findings; and in your argumentation, you're talking about the Lap mosque in Pristina. This is something that I think was touched upon during your direct testimony. Do you find that one?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You said there's no confirmation that the Lap mosque in Pristina was damaged during the war because, during the war no structure, monument, in Pristina suffered except from the consequences of the bombing of the centre. Now, I think, when you testified earlier, you told us that you were proud of the fact that no religious building in Pristina suffered damage during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And there was some discussion about what is referred to by some people as the Lap mosque in Pristina, and you said there was conflicting information about that in Riedlmayer's report and some other report. What other report were you referring to or do you know?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this is the report where Mr. Heymowski is mentioned, who was a consultant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to show you what's been marked as Exhibit P3145, and I'm sorry I don't have a translation in Serbian. I will describe this to you, and maybe you can tell me if it's the one you're thinking of. It's dated as the 7th of November, 2006, a document adopted by the Ministry of Culture, Youth, and Sports in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think we need to go to page 2 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It's described as a preliminary technical assessment of the architectural and archaeological heritage in south-east Europe. And in the forward, it mentions several experts ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: ... including Emma Carmichael from the United Kingdom, Giorgio Gianighian from Italy, Heymowski from Sweden, and some others. Is that the report you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I don't know if you can see a photograph there, but this is a photograph that purports to be of the mosque of Lap in Pristina. Item number 1.5 lists an address for that mosque as Ilir Konushevci Street. Does that help refresh your memory about where this particular mosque was located?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That mosque is on the road leading out of Pristina towards Podujevo, to the best of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So you were familiar with this mosque?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, I am, but there's a confusion of concepts. In Mr. Riedlmayer and Herscher's reports, there's a mention of the dzamija, the mosque at Vranjevac. I don't know whether they're referring to Lap dzamija or the Vranjevac dzamija, because to the best of my knowledge it says, on the 13th, one mosque, not two mosques, in Pristina were damaged. Now you have information that there's one mosque and the other mosque, so which one are they referring to? Because not even the experts who brought this information, they probably had Riedlmayer's report, and I surprised they didn't compare it with their finding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, here's a photograph and the report describes in some detail the damage, primarily consisting of a fire in the interior and all the woodwork being charred and ruined. So the mosque is not destroyed but it's damaged. My point is it's not whether it's one or two, but you said there was not a single religious building in Pristina that was damaged during the war. Here we have a report, we have a paragraph, we have a committee of experts doing an assessment, and the report indicates that this mosque in Pristina was damaged during the war. Do you disagree with that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Prosecutor, I think I was precise in my answer, I was very precise. I said in the course of wartime operations. On the 13th, there is no war; the war had ended before that. You have to understand something that's part of one's intimate feelings. Everybody finds this very difficult. If I say something with pride, you have to understand me. You have to know that I'm attached to something in peacetime but not to the tragedy of any group or nation. You shouldn't take it like that. This is a totally unprotected mosque. It's actually a market-place, a bazaar. This is a bazaar mosque. There's no fence around it or anything. When there was a market, they had thousands of people gathered around.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Stop. But you said, earlier in your testimony, not a single religious building in Pristina was damaged during the war. This is a religious building and this report indicates it was damaged during the car. Are you saying the damage happened five minutes after the war ended? What's your information about when it happened?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it happened on the same day the archives were damaged or the next day because that's a little bit further away from the archives, so I wasn't able to see it for myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But you have no personal knowledge or information to dispute the report's finding that it was damaged during the war, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly not in the course of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How do you know that? You weren't there. You have no personal information.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Prosecutor, I communicated with my Albanian colleagues on a daily basis. They were in the museum building with me, and it was from them I would hear information that something like that had happened. I was constantly in communication with them; and, therefore, I was always at the source of information. So please don't put me in this uncomfortable situation. Everything has its limits. Don't attack a person's personality.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were your Albanian colleagues going out and checking on the mosque of Lap on a regular basis prior to the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, I was in daily communication with those people. They were with me --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. My question was: Were they going out and doing a check on the Lap mosque prior to the end of the war, so they would be able to know if anything had happened to it?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was not their official duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, I would ask Mr. Hannis to point to a reference where there's a finding by the commission that it was damaged during a certain point in time. From my review of the document, it appears they are only relying upon Sabri Bajgora again.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document speaks for itself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In your testimony yesterday, the page which was then numbered 50, you talked about the ethnic breakdown of employees at the library [sic]. Who held the higher positions -- I'm sorry. Not the library, the museum. Who held the higher positions in the library [sic] in 1998 and 1999 when you were the director, and what ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a Turkish lady at the library.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. What was her name?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Why --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Bukrija [phoen].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which library are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I meant at the museum.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're away on a tangent, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The museum library, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And regarding the positions, you said, at page 55: "From 1975 until 1990, the dominant leading staff was made of Albanians; however, then certain changes came about and the political situation was that it was what it was and changes were implemented." So, after 1990, the changes that resulted, resulted in Serbs holding the vast majority of the higher positions throughout Kosovo, right?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the political situation that existed. I would rather refrain from commenting it because I know that that might provoke your anger. So I would rather refrain from any comments. If you wanted to hear me out, then I could tell you everything from the beginning to the end. I'm quite prepared to do that, as I have no reservations about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I feel --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry if my anger is bothering you, but my question was: Was the result of that change that you described that there were more --

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not used to that type of communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My question was: As a result of that change, was the result that Serbs held the vast majority of higher positions throughout Kosovo and Metohija? Can you say yes or no?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not have complete information. I suppose that that's how it was because the political process led in that direction. There were events happening of political nature. If you wish me to comment upon, then I can explain, but then don't interrupt me. Let me say it from the beginning to the end, so that you have complete insight into it. It was evident, and it was well-known to the international community, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You've answered my question. I'm not going to ask you that other one. You mentioned that in -- I'm not sure if I got it right in the transcript. In Pristina, is there an imperial mosque or was there an imperial mosque in 1999?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You did not misunderstand.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there also a mosque named the emperor's mosque or is that the same thing?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not find reference to emperor's mosque in the existing documentation.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You told us yesterday, at page 61, when we were talking about annex 8 to your statement, with the list of monuments, you said there were only two that were declared cultural property and that were created between 1901 and 1913. One of those was the imperial mosque in Pristina. Now, are you saying that mosque was built between 1901 and 1913?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says for the mosque in Gnjilane and for the imperial mosque in Pristina. That fact comes from the documentation and I quoted it. Those are the only two monuments from the 20th century that were put on the list of cultural heritage out of all monuments existing in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're -- you have no information to indicate that that mosque was built many, many years earlier, hundreds of years earlier?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can only speak on the basis of the existing documentation, and that's what the documentation says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, you can't. No, you can't. You're a man who's familiar with Pristina, you know the layout of the place, the cultural buildings within it. Please answer that question. Is there nothing you know of to indicate the mosque was built earlier than that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I truly don't have any piece of information on the basis of which I could tell you what year the mosque was built, except for what the documentation says. If we were to do some other kind of expertise, perhaps that figure or that date could be different. But I don't have anything else that could help me make a different conclusion. I found documents stating that those are the only two monuments from the 20th century that were put on the list of cultural property.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Have you never heard it suggested anywhere by anyone that that mosque is older?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I had no occasion. It is possible that is different, but you need to show me relevant information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, I'm asking you. Have you never heard it suggested anywhere by anyone that that mosque is older?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, by your leave, let me just give you a sentence. It's a very tragic situation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. If I may explain in a sentence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I hope it's short.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- by your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's a simple, straightforward answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly. Neglect and lack of care in relation to cultural monuments has been present for decades, both on the part of ethnic communities that use those buildings and also on the part of the protection services. This is a tragic situation, and it shouldn't be attributed to any individual. It's a general state of affairs. This is the lack and neglect that is not present elsewhere in Europe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please stop. I note your unwillingness to answer my question. I have other questions I'll deal with in a moment. Mr. Hannis, are you about finished?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. I just have a couple more questions on this, and then one about some listings in the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, let's focus this and get it complete.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: There's a limit to the time we can spend on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of the imperial mosque referred to as the mosque of Sultan Mehmed the II?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It probably has two names, but I don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're not aware that others have claimed it was built in 1461?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not come across that fact in the report by Riedlmayer and Herscher, so I did not do any further research. I simply used what they had and I compare it to other documents. I don't know how else I can explain that to you. If they who used the database by Mr. Bajgora didn't come to that conclusion, then I was even less likely to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you're not aware of it being listed as a protected monument in 1953 rather than 1993?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never claimed it was in 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, you did. Isn't that what you said yesterday?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document which we presented is dated 31st December, 1994, but it doesn't mean that it was created on that date. That is -- that is covering the overall situation of the protected monuments from after the Second World War, and there has been a very clear answer on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just a moment. Mr. Hannis, your question at 65, line 7, has been not fully transcribed. I think you made a reference to the sultan. No, no, sorry. It's line 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sultan Mehmed the II. My spelling on the document I had was M-e-h-m-e-d.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if I may be of assistance, I think that later on I noticed that in transcript there was a mistake. The witness said "1953" and transcript reads "1993," and we can listen to the tapes. I think that this is where the confusion was created.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What's the line reference for that, Mr. Bakrac?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't have the line. I simply looked at it in haste yesterday. I noticed that it was a mistake, but I will check it with my people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. A law of diminishing returns, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please get this completed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, in preparing your report and/or in preparing your testimony here, did you review the indictment in this case, in particular paragraph 75(d) [sic] which listed a number of mosques that the Prosecution alleges were destroyed during the war?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Not 75(d), I don't think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 77(d).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I misspoke.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't consider it necessary to review that. My belief was that that indictment or simply focusing on that kind of material would lead me in an inappropriate direction. All I evaluated was the report before me, that by Mr. Riedlmayer and Herscher. I didn't go into the nature of other issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You're aware that one of the allegations is that the mosque in Bela Crkva was damaged during the war, that the minaret was destroyed?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the documentation offered by Mr. Riedlmayer and Mr. Herscher, that's what stems from it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you have no evidence to dispute that, do you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't get to the relevant information. I wasn't invited to visit these sites, nor would it be possible for me to do that. I would gladly do that were it possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You didn't see the aerial photographs before and after of Bela Crkva, showing a mosque with a minaret standing and then later on without a minaret? You didn't see that photograph?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most likely I did see it, but I stand by what I have stated earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you didn't read the testimony of the eye-witnesses from that area about the mosque being damaged, did you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read some statements, maybe even that particular one. You now want to deal with the situation that I cannot describe because I lack relevant information. I was on the spot watching the archives burn, and you don't believe me because you don't consider me to be a reliable eye-witness. So you're using double standards. If you don't believe me who was present on the spot, how could I trust somebody else? Perhaps that witness is right, but I have no evidence to support or deny it. All I'm doing is using available sources, unless somebody told me to do otherwise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, Mr. Hannis has not suggested he doesn't believe you; it's not his job to believe you or otherwise. You have no basis for making that conclusion, and the only evidence you've been able to give us was that it was on fire. You have given no indication of who set it on fire. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Professor, I do believe you that it burned. I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have found it. It's page 25838, line 20. I think it would be good to listen to the tapes. The witness said "1953," and the transcript reads "1993."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We shall ask CLSS to revise that line.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Professor, was any part of the Pristina museum moved to Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was exhibited at the exhibition called archaeology and the other exhibition, jewellery and gold artefacts, that was in 1998, late 1998, and early 1999. It was moved, and also certain artefacts from the ethnographic collection were moved, pursuant to approval of General Jackson based on The Hague Convention on immunity of cultural heritage. Since we were conducting revision of material, that material was in the whole of the museum; and after the 12th -- or rather, the 10th of June, I can't remember the exact date, but some ten or 15 days later the building was broken into, and there was a danger that material could be destroyed. I managed to protect the material and the British unit within KFOR assisted us in housing and protecting that material. This --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what proportion of the artefacts of the museum were ultimately in Belgrade rather than Pristina?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: About 5 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is it you do then?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: 5 per cent of the total collection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what is it you do as the director of the Pristina museum when you can't actually get to Pristina?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We work with the existing collection, the collection that's available to us. We also produce technical documentation and other kinds of documentation. This is a lot of work for curators. Those who work in the field know that it's not the kind of work that can be completed in a short period of time. It requires long-term work because everything needs to be put on digital form and documented and put in the appropriate space. Also conservation or preservation of the material, that's another demanding work that is quite labour-intensive.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: How many of a staff do you have?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have those who are employed and those who are not. Technical personnel is not employed and the professional staff are. There are six of those who are employed, and the others are on what we call waiting. They are technical personnel, such as doormen and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So do they work with you?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Technical personnel is officially still engaged, but they do not work because it's technically not possible. We are using a building that already has such technical services, so we do not need to actually use the services of our own technical people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are there any Muslim artefacts among the 5 per cent of the collection that you have?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have artefacts that are archaeological and ethnographic. When it comes to archaeological artefacts, it is neither Islamic or Christian, it is European. That is the only way I can describe it. As for the ethnographic artefacts, they are somehow classified, categorised when we were doing the review. Also when we were moving that from the museum building --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So is the answer no? Try and make it simple for me.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will explain it in one sentence. That material is of general importance. It contains jewellery and costumes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I never, for a moment, suggested that archaeological artefacts should necessarily fall under one religious denomination description or another. I just wanted to know if any of the artefacts you have of any type whatsoever are of a particularly Islamic connection. That's all.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What was used for the exhibition in Belgrade in 1998, among that material, you can find some artefacts, most likely. As for the part that had been moved with the assistance of the British army, there is no other artefacts included there because their expert followed the -- monitored the classification of the material. So it was nobody's intention that it be done that way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please listen carefully to this question and try to answer it yes or no, if you can. Do you consider yourself to be an expert in Muslim religious buildings?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. We will take another break at this stage. We have to break for half an hour at this stage, Professor. So could you again please leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. Could you please leave the courtroom with the usher. We'll see you again at -- we'll try to make it ten minutes to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Very short, Your Honour. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Professor, in the course of the

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: attached to Riedlmayer and Herscher report. In your report at the last page, there is annex 11, where it is stated in the list of objects seen -- contained in the database Herscher/Riedlmayer. Have you compiled the list or not and is it based on the said database?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Have you, as a part of this list that you had formed that's part of the present annex 11, did you include the photographs that are related to specific objects and locations?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. In your report on page 21, 5.5, 21, page 21, in the column arguments, argumentation, under 23, have you found that?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you here find that it's a problem that the gentlemen, Herscher and Riedlmayer, failed to verify the credibility of the information?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my complaint in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you're saying that information received from a certain source needs to be verified if possible?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. My last two questions. Page 30, page 30, 5.6, in relation to number of Islamic mosques and Islamic monuments in Pec, are Messrs. Riedlmayer and Herscher getting confirmation in relation to their claim that the number of Islamic monuments that were attacked on the -- in the relevant period, do they give argumentation whether they were attacked or not?

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they don't give any proof.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My last question -- or rather, I don't have any further questions. Thank you, Professor.

utterances.speaker: BRANIMIR JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zecevic. There are a number of issues here over what ought to be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The report reminds us about references made to other reports. I think there are six others, Mr. Zecevic, that are referred to in pages 5 to 7, I think, of -- or to page 8 of the report. Are these all exhibits already in the trial?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe so. They are --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. Your Honour, I believe they are just annexes to the report; and in the very end of his report, you have the document which lists all 15 annexes to the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So, are these six annexes to the present report?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the report, there are references to a number of documents which are neither annexes nor existing exhibits in the case. What is it you expect us to do in relation to them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you take page 13 in the English, and you'll see at the top in the right-hand column the reference to Branislav Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What are we to make of that?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, since Professor Jokic is our joint expert, I would -- if I would be given until tomorrow morning so I can consult with other Defences, I'll then propose to the Trial Chamber our view of the issue -- on the issue of how possibly we can deal with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The annexes have been referred to, to a limited extent, in the evidence and are referred to also, to a limited extent, in the report itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yeah, that is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We see no reason why this whole documentation should be admitted. We have to be selective about what happens here now that the case is so focused.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have identified, during the direct and the cross-examination and the Trial Chamber questions, I have identified actually five annexes which have been referred to. But still I would, as I explained, I would need to consult with my colleagues on a proposal which we would make to the Trial Chamber, if you permit me to do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: If you take as an example annex 5 which is, Project for the protection of natural and cultural heritage in Metohija, hopefully all that is required from that is perhaps an example of something indicating methodology --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Exactly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- bearing in mind that it deals with -- well, virtually everything it deals with is not an issue in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is -- it is an example of methodology and I referred to, I believe, only four or five e-court pages, and we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- certainly accommodate the Trial Chamber in that respect, the annex 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So what you're suggesting is that you make a filing on this, are you?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, whatever pleases the Court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can do it orally as well tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. It would be satisfactory if you were to make a filing, bearing in mind what we've said --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I understand, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- and ensuring that what's submitted does justice to your position. And since you can, obviously, dedicate yourself to this while others deal with other evidence, it would be very helpful to us if it could be done by the end of the day tomorrow. I appreciate that's quite a significant exercise, but you can appreciate why it would help us. It would enable those assisting us to get to grips with it, and give you an order fairly quickly, I hope, if there's anything that's controversial in there so that you know exactly where you stand on the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We're grateful for the indication that you will do all in your power to achieve that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I will do all in my power to achieve that. I was just wondering if the dead-line could be extended to Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. I was rather under the impression that Friday might not be a working --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I know. It's a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- day for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is not a working day, but what can I say, Your Honour? You understand as well as I do. I will definitely try to have that by end of Thursday; but in case we need to file it and we can have it on Friday, that would be certainly helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think so that you have flexibility - it's obviously in your own interests to do it as quickly as possible - but so that you have flexibility in what you're doing to allow you some flexibility in doing this, we'll require that you make that filing by Monday so that you have time at the weekend if necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm very much obliged to Your Honours. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, Mr. Hannis, if it looks controversial, we'll expect a quick response from you, but it may turn out that it's not a controversial issue. But you will receive an e-mail once we see it indicative of when we need a response, and that will depend on just how controversial it looks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would indicate, perhaps to save Mr. Zecevic something, I don't oppose the admission of annex 11, but I am opposed to all the others, so if I could have until, I don't know, a week from the following Monday to reply, because I'm going to be gone for the next few days, or at least Friday of next week. I think I'm back on Wednesday night, so I could have Thursday to work on it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Professor Jokic, that completes your evidence. I dare say you have spent two more restful days in your life than these two. The subject we find interesting but very detailed, and we're trying our best to focus on what really matters for this particular case. So thank you for coming to assist us. You may now leave the courtroom with the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I hope I was of assistance to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, the floor may be yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you, Your Honour. Dr. Fruits, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, I hope you are sure of the "Fruits."

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Sure of the fruits, Your Honour? You mean as opposed to the nuts?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Well, I think we sometimes are scared of nut cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Your Honour. The older I get, Your Honour, the less I understand; that's the only thing I'm certain of.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Dr. Fruits.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You're about to be examined by Mr. Sepenuk. You are both speaking English. Your answers and his questions have to be interpreted into a number of other languages. It's very helpful to the interpretation process if you concentrate on doing two things in particular. One is speaking more slowly than you are used to, and you are clearly a fast speaker I can tell already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Oh, my goodness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And, secondly, after Mr. Sepenuk completes the question, please delay a little before you begin to answer it to enable the interpreter to catch up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Dr. Fruits, that's one of my many defects. I speak too quickly, so I think both of us should try as much as possible to keep the pace measured and slower. Is that all right with you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Dr. Fruits, 3D893 is your report of 3 February 2008. If you would testify today before the Court, would you repeat everything that was stated in that report?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes, with one exception. In my report, I believe it's on page 23, I say that Dr. Ball does not indicate whether he attempted to obtain any information on NATO bombing from NATO itself. After reviewing the transcript of his testimony, I would like to change my report slightly to say that Dr. Ball indicated that he did not attempt to obtain any data from NATO regarding NATO bombings, and he did not attempt to either directly by himself or through the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, that is the subject of a supplemental information sheet that was submitted to the Court on 21 April, 2008.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And aside from that one correction, Dr. Fruits, in your report, you would testify today the same today?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Exhibit 1 to your report is your curriculum vitae. I'm not going to go through it in detail. Would you briefly summarize for the Trial Chamber your academic training in statistics?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes. I have a Ph.D. in economics and a master's degree in economics. I also have a bachelor's degree in business economics in public policy. As part of my graduate training, I spent a substantial amount of time studying econometrics, which is the application of statistics to economics issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Have you taught statistics?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. As an adjunct professor, I taught a graduate-level course in statistics that focused on the identifying and correcting for some of the common problems that one may come across in a linear regression analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And do I dare ask what is a linear regression --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, you're already falling into the trap of taking up immediately when the witness completes his answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Absolutely right, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So let's have a brief time out and start again.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's the last time it will happen, Your Honour, I promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Dr. Fruits --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: May you be struck down before it happens.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: It will never happen again, Your Honour, I promise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Dr. Fruits.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: What is a linear regression model?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Linear regression is simply one method that you can use statistics to either test the relationship between two or more variables or to quantify the relationships between two or more variables.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you teach now, Dr. Fruits?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. I teach a graduate-level course in urban economics at Portland State University.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I understand that you've recently started your own consulting business. Where were you previously employed?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: It was a firm called --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just give it that pause, please --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- or we will get into a real fankle and then have to go back over the evidence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The firm was called ECO North-west or Econ North-west. It was an economic consulting firm. I have now formed my own consulting firm that focuses on economics, finance, and statistical consulting.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Have you published peer review papers using statistical techniques?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do the fundamentals and the approaches to statistical analysis vary with the topic being studied?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: No. You can think of statistics as a tool; and as with any tool, the tool itself doesn't necessarily change with what the issue is at hand. Instead, the innovations are how you apply that tool to the issue at hand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Beside from teaching and the publication of papers and articles, do you regularly engage in consulting projects which use statistical techniques?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And have any of these projects involved statistical analysis of demographic data?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes, they have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what is demographic data?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Demography is simply the study of the composition of human populations and the changes in the composition of human populations. So demographic data is just data about the human population that you're studying.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you have engaged in these kinds of projecting, these kinds of analyses?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Have you been admitted as a statistical expert in courts of the United States?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes, I have. I have been admitted as a statistical expert in US courts, and I have provided testimony on behalf of both plaintiffs and defendants.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, Dr. Fruits, you've been jointly retained by the defendants in this case. What was your assignment in this matter?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: My assignment was to review the testimony and reports of Dr. Patrick Ball and to provide an opinion regarding his conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: According to Dr. Ball, there are three possible hypotheses to explain refugee flow and killings. What are those hypotheses?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: One hypothesis is that they were caused by KLA activities; a second hypothesis is that they were caused by NATO activities, specifically air-strikes or bombing; and the third hypothesis is that it was some sort of a coordinated or systematic activity by Serb or Yugoslav forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: With respect to the third hypothesis, Dr. Fruits, acts of Serb forces, Dr. Ball concludes as follows, and I'm quoting now from P1506, Dr. Ball's report of 3 January 2002, on page 1. I quote from Dr. Ball: "The statistical evidence is consistent with the hypothesis that Yugoslav forces conducted a systematic campaign of killings and expulsions." I ask you, Dr. Fruits, do you agree with that conclusion; and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: I do not agree with that conclusion. The main reason why I do not is because Dr. Ball does not analyse any data on Serb or Yugoslav forces' activities; and, indeed, I believe he indicated in his testimony that he was -- he didn't have any data on Serb or Yugoslav forces' activities, and that any data that was available was sparse or patchy and not sufficient to conduct any analysis with.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And without reliable information on Serb force activities by date and time, is it possible statistically to draw any conclusions regarding the activities of Serb forces to Kosovo migration, Kosovo Albanian migration?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: No, you cannot. And I believe I mention in my report, I think it's on pages 33 and 34, that without any sort of reliable data on Serb and Yugoslav forces' activities, that one cannot draw any statistically reliable conclusions about those activities and whether or not they affected deaths and migration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And you go into that in more detail in your report, do you not, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Let's assume, Dr. Fruits, that all the other variables we've talked about, deaths, migration, KLA and NATO activities, let us assume that these were all appropriately measured. Given that assumption, sir, without information on Serb force activities, is it statistically possible to conduct a reliable study?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: No, you cannot. If the hypothesis is that Serb and Yugoslav forces' activities contributed to the deaths and migration, without the Serb forces' activities you cannot conduct a statistically reliable study. In fact, by omitting that variable, by leaving out the Serb forces' activities, you are -- you are committing an error known as an omitted variable error. And it generates biases, not just in the data that's missing, but it also causes your estimates of the impacts of the KLA and the NATO activities to also be unreliable; in other words, they may not reflect reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: In Dr. Ball's report, and this is P1506, at page 15, his report of 3 January 2002, he points to a unilateral cease-fire on April 6/7 by the Yugoslav authorities in recognition of the Orthodox Easter as a "circumstantial link" to show that, and again here quoting from Dr. Ball: "To show that when Yugoslav forces ceased hostilities, the number of killings and refugee departures fell drastically." Do you agree with this conclusion of Dr. Ball about a circumstantial link to Serb force activity; and if you don't agree, if you don't agree, why don't you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: I don't agree with Dr. Ball regarding the -- what he calls the circumstantial link. As I mention in my report, I don't recall which page, I think the more obvious reason why the number of -- number of people crossing the Morina border declined was simply because the border was closed. Also regarding the number of deaths declining, I believe it's on page 28 of my report, I use some of Dr. Ball data to show that, in fact, deaths were higher on the 6th and 7th than they were in the two-day period prior or the two-day period after. So the conclusion that deaths actually were lower on April 6th and 7th is simply not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Just to fill in a little gap there, because you frankly anticipated my next question, which was Dr. Ball's testimony that during the cease-fire the number of deaths "falls towards 0 or towards 0." Your conclusion in that regard is, briefly?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: My conclusion is that the number of deaths do not fall; in fact, they increase over the period April 6th and 7th. Let me make that more clear. On April 6th and 7th, the deaths are actually higher than in the two days before or the two days after.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: That's, by the way, set forth in more detail on page 28 of your report; is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I ask you one question about the omitted variable error. Assuming Dr. Ball carries out the exercise in exactly the way he's done it, but separately evidence is led here of activities of Serb and Yugoslav forces which turns out to be consistent with the hypothesis that he finds to be consistent with killings and expulsions, is his work equally invalid because he did not personally take into account information about the movements and activities of Serb and Yugoslav forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that would be a fair assessment. Let me try to paraphrase what you've said because I think I understand the question. Dr. Ball's analysis would still be invalid even if there was evidence here that may support his conclusions simply because that the information that may support his conclusions hasn't actually been included in his analysis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: To a layman that might actually be, on the face of it, a feature that validates his approach, that he does something scientific that turns out to be consistent with what the evidence might portray, the evidence of what happened on the ground; whereas, if he took account of information about what had happened on the ground, it might be thought by the layman that that was a circular argument, that it was a self-fulfilling prophecy.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can -- I see what you're getting at. The difficulty I have as a statistician is that you really can't come to a conclusion in a round-about way, in which Dr. Ball does, in which you simply reject two other alternative explanations and then come to a conclusion that it must be a third alternative, in this case the third alternative being the coordinated efforts of Serb or Yugoslav forces. I think your question is: Is it okay for Dr. Ball to exclude the and Yugoslav forces and activity to avoid the circularity? I didn't really investigate any of the other information in this case, including, for example, from the fact witness. My focus was narrowly on Dr. Ball's statistical analysis; and as a statistician, his statistical analysis isn't reliable simply because it doesn't have that information on the Serb and Yugoslav forces' activity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So just to summarize on this issue, Dr. Fruits, is there a circumstantial link, in your opinion, between Yugoslav force activities and the refugee flow and killings of Albanian citizens?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Let's turn to the following conclusion of Dr. Ball in his report, this is P1506, again the report of 3 February 2002, page 1, he concludes as follows, and I quote: "Two of the hypothesis proposed to explain the patterns in killing and migration, KLA and NATO activities are inconsistent with the observed pattern of refugee flow and killings." And that's unquote. Do you agree with this conclusion, Dr. Fruits; and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: I disagree with that conclusion, the reason being that the data that he constructs of KLA and NATO activities is fundamentally flawed, and those flaws make it impossible or very difficult to reach any sort of reliable conclusions using any analysis of that data.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Let's start with the KLA. What's wrong with that data, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Dr. Ball has two measures of KLA activities: One is what he calls KLA battles and another one is what he calls KLA killings. KLA battles he provides a variety of definitions of: One is simply a battle which is, according to the dictionary I consulted, a sustained fight between two armies. Another definition of a battle that Dr. Ball uses is he calls an exchange of fire. And those two definitions really highlight some of the difficulties in the KLA battle data that Dr. Ball relies on, in that there's no measure of the intensity of the battles, in that an exchange of fire between two people is given the same weight as a sustained battle that may have a number of casualties. The other problem is in what he calls the KLA killing data, which really isn't -- it's more than just killings. It includes kidnappings, also injuries, and I believe what he calls disappearances of Serbs in what he describes as isolated incidents. It's not entirely clear what an isolated incident is, and it's not entirely -- and, again, as with KLA battle data, there's no measure of the intensity or the scale of these -- of these variables.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. Is there any analogy that might be appropriate here?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Well, you can think of, if you're trying to study, say, crop yields and you want to see the effect of rainfall on crop yields, it's not just enough to know whether it rained on a given day. You really need to know how much it rained. Dr. Ball's approach gives the same weight to a raindrop as it would to a downpour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Where did Dr. Ball get his data on KLA activities?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: In my report, I note that Dr. Ball's report states that he received the data from the OTP; however, he doesn't really provide a description of how he converts that data from the OTP or the information from the OTP into quantifiable data with which he can do his analysis.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: So from the data presented by Dr. Ball, is it possible for you to verify the reliability and accuracy of the KLA data?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Let's turn now to the hypotheses of Dr. Ball that NATO activity was inconsistent with the observed patterns of refugee flow and killings. Do you agree with this conclusion of Dr. Ball's, sir; and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: I disagree with that conclusion of Dr. Ball's; and one reason is, again, as with the KLA data, he has no measure of the intensity of the NATO air-strikes, but also he mismeasures or miscounts the number of air-strikes that occurred on given days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And does your Exhibit 8 go into that in a little more detail?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. Exhibit 8 to my report shows that there were six dates in which Dr. Ball's data indicates or Dr. Ball's data reports that there were no NATO air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Can you just pause there for a second. I know you haven't completed your answer. I simply wanted to find out whether in Dr. Ball -- in your report, there were a number of strikes that were reported that Dr. Ball didn't report; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I'll go into detail just in another couple of minutes?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
