utterances.text: There's a specific question I want to cover that with. All right. And by the way, did you compare NATO's publicly available information during this period with the data prepared by Dr. Ball?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. So you did make those comparisons?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. And when, to your knowledge, did NATO make this information publicly available?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Approximately March of 2000.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, I'll get to the question that you were -- you were answering just 30 seconds ago. In his report Dr. Ball states as follows, this is P1506, again 3 January 2002 report, page 13, he says, and I quote: "One other noteworthy fact regarding NATO air-strikes was that during 2-4 April attacks were greatly reduced due to bad weather, yet this period during which there were relatively few NATO air-strikes included substantial peaks in Kosovo-wide killings and refugee flows." Do you agree with that observation of Dr. Ball, Dr. Fruits; and if not, why not?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Well, I disagree with that statement because, in the main, what Dr. Ball says were greatly reduced air-strikes were actually much higher than were in his own data. NATO over that same period reported approximately ten air-strikes. Dr. Ball's data reported only two.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Now, how important would it be to know the intensity of the NATO air-strikes, and did Dr. Ball's data provide this information?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: No. Dr. Ball indicated in his report that he did not have any measure of the intensity of the air-strikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And that's also important, is it? Is the rainfall analogy also applicable here?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes. It's very similar, in the sense that, again, you need to know -- it would be more useful to know the intensity of an air-strike rather than just whether it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: In short, Dr. Fruits, does Dr. Ball's analysis of NATO air-strikes provide the kind of reliable information necessary regarding the cause for migration and deaths in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: No, it doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Okay. What we've talked about so far are three hypotheses that may explain Kosovo Albanian deaths and migration. Are there other hypotheses; and if so, what are they?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: There are some other hypotheses, for example, the announcement of NATO air-strikes; for example, warning that air-strikes were going to occur may have prompted migration. Similarly, I understand from the testimony in Dr. Ball's -- Dr. Ball's testimony that there was some indication that the KLA may have either made announcements or threats or urgings for people to leave an area, and those sorts of announcements are another hypothesis of causes of migration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And I should mention, I believe this is correct, you talked about the individual decision-making perhaps being motivated by the threat of credible NATO air-strikes; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Is there a hypothesis of rational expectations? Does that ring a bell with you?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes. In economics, there's a theory or a principle called rational expectations. A gentleman by the name of Robert Lucas received the Nobel prize for developing this theory, and it's a relatively straightforward theory. It simply says that people take into consideration expectations, and those expectations can be formed by announcements, threats, or promises.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I would like to turn now to the data on migration and deaths, and Dr. Ball states, at P1506 again, page 4, he says: The patterns of migration and deaths are a key component of his findings." Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: No, I disagree with that. Dr. Ball concludes that there's patterns and that the two series, the series of death and migration, are correlated; however, he never does the statistical procedure called a correlation analysis. Instead, he merely eyeballs the two series and then jumps to the conclusion that they are correlated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: You've used the expression eyeballing a few times in your report. What do you mean by eyeballing?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Well, eyeballing is an ad hoc or a subjective look-see at the -- at two series, and rather than any sort of rigorous test of whether or not the two series are correlated. So just like we can look at -- we can look at the same cloud formation and I might see a castle and you might see a bunny rabbit, two people can look at the same picture, and same graph, and one person can see correlation and other people can see no correlation.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you have an example of eyeballing that might be useful for the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Yes. I think it would be useful to start with figure 2 from Dr. Ball's corrigendum.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honours, that's P1394, page 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: And what is that, Dr. Fruits?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: This is the -- this is the series of migration and deaths from Dr. Ball's corrigendum. I believe this figure is similar to the figure in his main report. Then what I did is I took this figure, this figure 2, and then just simply added some straight lines, and the purpose of adding those straight lines is to show that what one may think of --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting. Before you get to the straight lines, that's a separate exhibit, sir.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: The separate Exhibit is 3D1144, if that could be put right next to figure 2 on page 3 of P1394. If that's too difficult, you could simply put the exhibit up, 3D1144, because it's the same exhibit with an overlay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The registrar can't pick up that exhibit, Mr. Sepenuk.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I have a hard copy, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, can we put that on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: If, in fact, Your Honour, the 3D1144 was not uploaded into the system yesterday as I was told, another head will roll, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Do you have that on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: I have it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, tell us what this represents.

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: Well, it's the same figure, figure 2, only the vertical lines drawn on it were put in there by me. They're to show that whereas in the first case you might eyeball that graph and say that the two series are correlated or very similar, that when you look at them a little closer by drawing these lines, you see that there are some substantial differences between the two graphs. For example, on the left-hand side, you could see that the peaks in the people leaving their homes and the peaks in the number of deaths actually don't coincide, that they're separated by several days. Also, you could see right here in the middle that there's a small peak in the number of people leaving their homes, but there's a -- there's a sizeable decline in the number of reported deaths. Then the third instance would be over here, where you see --

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Over where, sir?

utterances.speaker: ERIC FRUITS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It's all the way to the right of that picture. You could see that there's a relatively high number of deaths on two different dates, but relatively flat or no refugee flows. And, again, the point of this is, to just illustrate, a quick glance at the graphs may lead one to conclude that they're correlated, but, indeed, some more sophisticated analysis is required to actually come to a conclusion that they are statistically correlated.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Can we get an ID number, Your Honour, and that should be a 3D number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is there, so it's 3D1144.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm going to guess that I have probably five to ten minutes, but I don't want to tax your patience. I could stop now or we can resume in the morning. Whatever Your Honour's pleasure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We would like you to finish your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just now. There is no case here this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, I may be wrong. Sorry, there is a case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I thought there is no case but apparently there is, so we have to break now, Mr. Sepenuk. I'm sorry about that. Dr. Fruits, we have to terminate today's sitting at this time because another case sits in this court in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That means you'll need to return tomorrow to finish your evidence, and that will be in a different courtroom. It will be in Court III --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please leave the court with the usher and we'll see you tomorrow at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
